summary: Finland lies in Northern Europe with tens of thousands of lakes and vast forests; it became independent from Russia in 1917 and is known for its education system and sauna culture.

ranking.name: Lutheranism
ranking.description: In the 12th–13th centuries the Kingdom of Sweden expanded eastward and brought Catholicism to Finland in the name of the crusades, and the legendary Bishop Henry is venerated as Finland’s patron. In the 1520s the Swedish king Gustav Vasa carried out the Reformation and Lutheranism became the state religion; the Finnish Reformation figure Mikael Agricola translated the New Testament into Finnish in 1548. The Evangelical Lutheran Church of Finland is still a national church and can levy church tax, but the new Freedom of Religion Act of 2003 made leaving the church simple, and the share of believers declines year by year.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Finland urbanized and secularized rapidly in the late 20th century, and the Nordic welfare state replaced the church’s role in social care. Since 2003 one can leave the church with a single click online, and whenever the church causes controversy over issues such as same-sex marriage, a wave of resignations follows; the non-religious population is concentrated in Helsinki and other cities and in the younger generation.

ranking.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
ranking.description: Orthodoxy originated in the medieval missionary work of Novgorod in the Karelia region and expanded further after Finland became a grand duchy of the Russian Empire in 1809–1917. The Orthodox Church of Finland is, like the Lutheran Church, a national church. After the Soviet Union took Karelia following World War II in 1944, about four hundred thousand evacuees (many of them Orthodox) were resettled across Finland, so Orthodox churches are found throughout the country.

religion.background: In the Middle Ages Sweden from the west and Novgorod from the east brought Catholicism and Orthodoxy to Finland respectively, making it the meeting point of the eastern and western Christian traditions. After the Reformation of the 16th century Lutheranism became the faith of the great majority, and it promoted the written use of Finnish and universal literacy (the Lutheran Church required believers to be able to read the Bible before they could marry). Russian rule after 1809 raised the status of Orthodoxy. After independence in 1917 the two churches were both national churches, but from the late 20th century Finnish society secularized rapidly and the non-religious population grew greatly.

language.official: Finnish and Swedish are the official languages.

ranking.name: Finnish
ranking.description: Finnish belongs to the Uralic family and has no kinship with Swedish or Russian. During six hundred years of Swedish rule, Swedish was the language of administration and the upper class, and in 1543 Agricola published the first Finnish primer. In 1835 Lönnrot compiled the national epic Kalevala, which stirred national consciousness, and in 1863 the Russian tsar Alexander II issued a language decree that gradually gave Finnish official status equal to Swedish; the 1919 constitution established Finnish as a national language.

ranking.name: Swedish
ranking.description: Swedes settled on the southwestern coast of Finland in the Middle Ages, and until 1809 Finland was part of the Kingdom of Sweden, so Swedish long dominated administration, education and culture. The 1919 constitution made Finnish and Swedish both national languages, and schools still require study of the second national language; the Swedish-speaking minority is concentrated along the coast and in the autonomous Åland Islands.

ranking.name: Russian
ranking.description: From 1809 to 1917 Finland was an autonomous grand duchy of the Russian Empire, but Russian was never widespread. Today’s Russian speakers come mainly from immigration after 1990, including the Ingrian Finnish “return migrants” whose entry President Koivisto opened up, concentrated in Helsinki and the eastern border towns.

ranking.name: Estonian
ranking.description: After Estonia restored independence in 1991 and joined the EU in 2004, large numbers of Estonians crossed the Gulf of Finland to work in Finland, and there are many commuters between the two capitals. Estonian and Finnish both belong to the Finnic branch and are close to each other, making it easy for Estonians to integrate into Finnish society.

language.history: The ancestors of Finnish were speaking it around the Gulf of Finland thousands of years ago, and from the Middle Ages Swedish rule made Swedish the language of the upper class, with Finnish only the spoken language of the peasants. At the Reformation Agricola devised a writing system for Finnish, and after Finland became a grand duchy of Russia in the 19th century, nationalists raised the status of Finnish through the Kalevala and the language movement, with the language decree of 1863 an important turning point. After independence in 1917, Finnish and Swedish became co-national languages, and Sami in the north gained legal status in the 1990s.

ranking.name: Karelian pie (Karjalanpiirakka)
ranking.description: A thin rye crust is wrapped around rice porridge, the edges pinched into a wavy pattern and baked, and eaten hot with egg butter (egg mixed with butter) spread on top.
ranking.history: The Karelian pie originated in the Karelia region on the border between eastern Finland and Russia; the early filling was barley or millet porridge, and rice was used only after imported rice became common in the 19th century. After the Soviet Union took Karelia following World War II in 1944, about four hundred thousand residents were evacuated across Finland and took this snack from home with them throughout the country, turning it from a regional food into a national favorite. Today it is everywhere in supermarkets, cafés and breakfasts, and has received EU Traditional Specialty Guaranteed protection.

ranking.name: Lohikeitto (salmon soup)
ranking.description: A milky, thick soup cooked from chunks of salmon, potato, leek and carrot with cream and plenty of dill, with a light and mild flavor.
ranking.history: Finland is called the “Land of a Thousand Lakes,” and with the long coastline of the Baltic Sea, fish has always been an important source of protein for Finns; lohikeitto was originally the everyday food of fishing families on the coast and in the lake districts. The version with cream reflects Finland’s well-developed dairy farming. It is a common dish at school lunches and family dinners and is the most representative warming soup of Finns during the long, cold winter.

ranking.name: Rye bread (ruisleipä)
ranking.description: A dark bread baked from rye flour fermented with sourdough for a long time, with a dense texture and pronounced sourness, sometimes made into round loaves with a hole in the middle.
ranking.history: Rye can grow in Finland’s cold, short summers and for hundreds of years has been the farmers’ staple. In the west the tradition was to make bread into round loaves with a hole in the middle, which after baking were strung on a long pole under the ceiling to dry and keep, being baked only a few times a year; in the east soft bread was baked every day. When Finland celebrated its centenary of independence in 2017, rye bread was voted Finland’s national food, which shows its place in Finnish hearts.

ranking.name: Kalakukko (fish pie)
ranking.description: Rye dough is wrapped around small fish (such as vendace or perch) and pork belly and baked for several hours until even the fish bones soften, and it can be cut open and eaten whole.
ranking.history: Kalakukko originated in the Savo region of eastern Finland and is most famous in Kuopio, where the many lakes yield abundant small fish. The thick rye crust protects the filling and makes it easy to carry and keep, and in the past it was the packed lunch of lumberjacks and farmers going out to work. Kuopio’s market still sells traditional kalakukko, and it is regarded as a symbol of Savo culture.

ranking.name: Mämmi (rye pudding)
ranking.description: A dark brown pudding made by cooking rye flour and malt with water and then baking, with the sweetness and slight bitterness of malt, eaten with cream and sugar.
ranking.history: Mämmi is a traditional Finnish Easter food that originated in southwestern Finland. In the past fire could not be lit for cooking on Good Friday, so people prepared in advance a pudding that could be eaten cold and kept it in boxes woven of birch bark. Although its appearance often puts foreigners off, in Finland it is a festival tradition of several hundred years, and every Easter supermarkets sell mämmi in cardboard packaging.
